blogs.title: One Marketplace, One Standard: The Federal Circuit Tells the TTAB to Keep Its DuPont Factors Aligned
blogs.description: This post would focus on the court’s central doctrinal move: once the Board found banking/financing services and credit card services highly similar—indeed partially legally identical—it could not then narrow the sixth DuPont factor to only third-party uses in the exact credit-card niche. The opinion matters because it pushes the TTAB toward a more internally consistent likelihood-of-confusion analysis and gives applicants a stronger basis to introduce third-party-use evidence from adjacent, not identical, service categories.

blogs.title: Old Identifications, New Industries: Why ‘Credit Card Services’ Carried So Much Weight in Apex Bank
blogs.description: This post would examine the court’s affirmance of the second DuPont factor and the Board’s broad construction of the legacy term ‘credit card services,’ a phrase no longer found in the ID Manual. It would explore how older registrations can still cast long shadows in modern fintech disputes, especially when historic service descriptions are interpreted to encompass issuing cards, account management, payment processing, and other functions now spread across banks, processors, and platform partners.

blogs.title: Strength Before Similarity: Why Third-Party ‘Aspire’ Uses May Change the Mark-Comparison Analysis
blogs.description: This post would analyze the court’s decision to vacate not only factor six but also factor one, on the theory that commercial strength and commercial impression are intertwined. The opinion underscores that mark similarity cannot be evaluated in a vacuum: if ‘Aspire’ is shown to be diluted across financial services, the scope of protection for ASPIRE may narrow, altering how ASPIRE and ASPIRE BANK should be compared in appearance, sound, connotation, and overall impression.

blogs.title: Trademark Law for a Modular Financial Industry: Apex Bank and the Problem of Who the Consumer Thinks Is the Source
blogs.description: This post would place the case in a broader market context, where credit card products are often created through partnerships among issuing banks, servicers, and branded programs. The court’s reasoning highlights how trademark doctrine adapts to an industry in which consumers encounter bundled financial products without knowing which entity sits behind the scenes, making source confusion plausible even when the parties do not directly compete in the traditional sense.
